about: The 54 windows his extension read Human Low on the live post (2026-11-05; feed https://www.pangram.com/feed/9e40aa8f-317c-4490-893d-9e99c839de88), read from the feed page on 2026-11-07. windows.text:
I’d still like to have sex.”
That may be candid about what you expect now.
Sex can make a child.
It feels like it’s filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally—maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. Refusing to name the relationship doesn’t make the responsibility disappear. What they don’t escape is the existential void created by another superficial fix.

Ours wasn’t superficial. It was just painfully uneven.
Here’s the funny thing many people don’t understand: labels don’t create commitment. They can still expose whether two people think they’re in the same relationship, which matters a lot.
True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label.
Why wouldn’t it?
windows.touched: S2 (his "Why wouldn’t it?"; Human Low in #48 too)

windows.text: I don’t need the answer to be that provision had nothing to do with attraction.
Helping carry somebody through temporary incapacity is different from becoming the permanent support system for a man who won’t take responsibility.
It comes from reading I’ve done as well.

If closeness was safe when you were little, maybe it does feel a bit like coming home. But if it came with neglect, abuse, or if people disappeared on you, you can get more attached and more freaked out at the same time.
That may mean the game worked without telling us whether the relationship will.
How did you repair afterward? What did you learn?
Has your judgment gotten better, or do you keep falling for the same stuff?
My own list isn’t especially flattering.
I’m impulsive.

The relationship can close off at exactly the point when both people most need a view from outside it.
Sometimes withdrawing isn’t wrong.
We need people who actually know both of us over time, well enough that the relationship isn’t the only reality in the room.
Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you.
When the BPD splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship.
Then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along.
That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem.
Based on what?
Sometimes I actually learned something.
Sometimes nothing changed except that now I’m attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.
I want us to keep seeing friends, have some kind of community around the relationship, and pick actual dates to ask how it’s going.
Otherwise it’s too easy for me to assume the relationship is going well because we’re already entangled.

It still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.
You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there, touch or smell feels wrong, your desire levels or kinks don’t fit, one person is sexually shut down, or the bodies just don’t connect.
Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it.
And bring each other out into the world.
Other times it’s hard to tell.
The problem is when the role takes over the relationship.
She still has to remain responsible for her life and keep reparenting herself.
It can run the other way too.
But enough moments become a pattern.
I find that intolerable.
Once one person has become the default caregiver and that’s taken for granted, it’s time to bring in other support, lest the romance collapse under the burden.
I can’t answer that for others, and I couldn’t always answer it for myself, but asking the question out loud is usually where it starts.
In ordinary life, I sometimes think of the woman as the engine and myself as the steering wheel.
She should not have to perform softness, helplessness, or cuteness every minute to prove she is feminine.
Then she can over-correct into needing nobody and make receiving care or letting a man lead feel like weakness.
A man receiving care doesn’t make him a child either.
They are private until the person decides to share them.
When somebody does share one, it can be an extraordinary act of trust.
Esther Perel makes the distinction that fantasy is play rather than a real-life request.
That laboratory evidence establishes the biological validity and uniqueness of the phenomenon.
Her jade-egg practice is a preliminary training for the cervical O: pelvic-floor strength, attention, and arousal without needing a partner.
windows.touched: S17 (AI in every check since; open)

windows.text: Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?
Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much outside support.
The problem is when we’re using the same words for two different futures.
Two people really are in love and want to build something together.

They can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life without pretending they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.
Then the questions change for me. If the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain?
Are we promising actions, or low-key pretending to promise permanent feelings?
Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?
Sometimes the pretending does more damage than an outside connection would have.
Some things were less mysterious.
